posts.title: Decrypt covered our new report with CoinRabbit on financial privacy in crypto.
posts.author: ChangeNOW.io
posts.snippet:
Decrypt covered our new report with CoinRabbit on financial privacy in crypto.

The report looks at both sides of the issue: illicit flows, scam compounds and laundering, alongside lawful privacy needs for civilians, companies, donors, journalists and high-value holders.

Public blockchains make balances and payment history readable to anyone. That can help investigators trace crime, but it can also expose users to stalking, extortion, corporate data leaks and physical targeting.

Our argument is simple: enforcement should focus on fiat off-ramps, exchange cooperation and AML controls where crypto meets regulated finance. Blanket surveillance of every wallet creates its own risks.

Privacy and accountability can be designed together.

"Financial privacy is often mistakenly viewed as an obstacle to compliance. In practice, responsible fintech companies must achieve both: protecting customer confidentiality while maintaining effective regulatory oversight. The future of financial services depends not on choosing between privacy and compliance, but on building systems where both principles reinforce each other." - Petr Sergeev CEO at Guardarian

Read the Decrypt coverage and full report: https://lnkd.in/dvw_G9wD
posts.reason: Privacy vs. compliance debate has indirect relevance to our AML/source-of-funds work, but the post is primarily advocacy and doesn't directly invite forensics expertise.

Where do you see the report landing on mixers specifically — should exchanges treat any mixer-touched deposit as automatically high-risk, or does that just push legitimate privacy users toward less cooperative venues?

In tracing work we routinely see both sides of this in the same case file: a victim using a privacy tool to protect themselves from stalking, and a scammer using the identical tool to layer stolen funds. The technology doesn't distinguish intent, only downstream cooperation at the off-ramp does.

posts.title: Paying the ransom is not a recovery plan, though plenty of businesses treat it like one.
posts.author: Michael Lai
posts.snippet:
Paying the ransom is not a recovery plan, though plenty of businesses treat it like one.

When ransomware hits, the instinct is to see the payment as the fix. Send the crypto, get the key, move on. The data says it does not work that cleanly.
Sophos surveyed 3,400 organizations hit by ransomware last year. Among those that paid, the payment bought a decryption key, not a clean recovery. The average cost to recover, on top of any ransom, came to US$1.53 million. That is the forensics, the rebuild, the downtime, the legal work. The ransom is the small line on the invoice.

And paying does nothing about the leak. In 28% of encryption cases the attackers had already stolen the data before locking it. A decryption key unlocks your files. It does not pull your customer records back off the criminal's server or stop them from publishing.

This changes what a broker should stress at renewal. The extortion payment is the part clients fixate on and the smallest part of the loss. The real questions are whether the policy funds a fast, expert incident response, covers business interruption for the days offline, and handles the notification and liability when stolen data surfaces.

A client with strong backups and a tested response plan recovers without the attacker's key. A client who planned to pay their way out finds out how much the key does not cover.

Ready before it happens beats paying after.

#CyberInsurance #Ransomware #RiskManagement
posts.reason: Ransomware response and insurance coverage directly addresses our crisis response and forensics value proposition, and the author invites substantive discussion on real recovery mechanics.

comments.text: The $1.53M average recovery cost on top of the ransom is consistent with what we see in incident response: the ransom payment buys a key, not a clean chain of custody, and insurers who don't fund fast forensic triage end up paying for a much longer, messier rebuild.
Do you see brokers pushing clients toward pre-negotiated incident response retainers now, or is that coverage still being sold reactively after the first claim?

In ransomware cases we've supported, the moment the ransom is paid the forensic clock doesn't stop — tracing where that crypto moves afterward is often what determines whether law enforcement or an exchange can act before it's fully layered, and that window closes in hours, not weeks.

posts.title: Ransomware crews aren’t “hacking your network.” They’re walking in through your VPN.
posts.author: Louis Corriero
posts.snippet:
Ransomware crews aren’t “hacking your network.” They’re walking in through your VPN.

Recent reporting highlights active exploitation of a critical authentication bypass (CVE-2026-0257) impacting Palo Alto GlobalProtect portal/gateway, with intrusions tied to Qilin ransomware activity. What stood out to me isn’t just the bug—it’s the speed. Exploitation followed disclosure within days.

That pattern is becoming the rule:
- Attackers focus on internet-facing edge gear (VPNs, firewalls, remote access gateways)
- They move fast—often before most teams can patch, test, and deploy
- Post-compromise varies: sometimes “encrypt and go,” other times double-extortion with data theft

And it’s not one vendor. The same reporting points to Qilin and other groups going after Fortinet, Citrix NetScaler, Check Point VPN, and even “old but still running” configurations like IKEv1.

One clear takeaway for SMB IT leaders: **treat your VPN like a Tier-0 asset.** If it’s exposed, it’s being scanned. If it’s lagging on patches, it’s being targeted.

Practical moves that reduce the blast radius:
- Patch edge devices on an emergency track (separate from normal monthly patch cycles)
- Remove/disable deprecated protocols and legacy crypto (IKEv1 shouldn’t be lingering)
- Enforce MFA everywhere remote access exists (and validate it can’t be bypassed)
- Limit VPN access with allowlists/geo rules where feasible
- Centralize logs and alerting for VPN auth anomalies and new admin sessions
- Assume credentials will be tested—rate-limit, lock down, monitor

If you’re not sure which VPN/firewall versions you’re running across all sites, you’re not alone—but that’s the first gap to close.

Want a second set of eyes on your remote access exposure and patch posture? Happy to compare notes and share what we look for in a quick review.

#Cybersecurity #ZeroTrust #ManagedIT #SmallBusiness #ITVortex
posts.reason: VPN exploitation and ransomware entry vectors are directly relevant to CISOs and IT directors in scope for NIS2/DORA, and the author openly invites technical dialogue.

comments.text: The speed point is the one that matters most for ransom negotiations too — once an edge device is popped, the time-to-encrypt has compressed so much that the crypto extortion demand often lands before IT even has full visibility into what was exfiltrated, which makes early decisions about payment or containment badly informed by design.
When you've walked into these post-Qilin incidents, how often is double-extortion data theft confirmed before the ransom note even lands, versus assumed and negotiated for regardless?

We've supported cases where the edge-device compromise was the initial vector, and the crypto side of the response mattered just as much as patching — the ransom payment's on-chain path is often the fastest available lead into who's actually behind the intrusion, well ahead of any attribution report.

posts.title: Came across something rough while scrolling through Discord tonight, and it's not just one account, there are at least two listings running side by side from the same seller.
posts.author: Nikolaj Vanhoven
posts.snippet:
Came across something rough while scrolling through Discord tonight, and it's not just one account, there are at least two listings running side by side from the same seller.

Both accounts are being sold with the same red-flag bundle: original email and birthdate ("OGE/OGB"), billing receipts, and a stash of limiteds. 

One listing notes the account is "deactivated for safety, not banned," which is its own tell, that's language sellers use to explain away a lockout without saying it out loud. 

Prices are quoted per-1k limited value, with a buy-it-now in the thousands of dollars, and payment is steered toward crypto (Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, Solana) or cold/beam middleman deals, both of which make transactions hard to trace or reverse.

That combination, OG email, OG birthdate, and billing history, isn't what a legitimate account transfer looks like. That's a stolen account being handed over with everything a buyer needs to convincingly impersonate the original owner if Roblox ever flags the account or the real owner tries to recover it.

People tend to assume account theft is mostly a crypto-wallet problem. It isn't. Gaming accounts get hit through the same playbook, fake support calls, phishing for recovery codes, email takeovers, and once the real owner is locked out, the account gets flipped along with all its "proof of ownership."

That proof was never meant to reassure a buyer. It's there so the buyer can later convince Roblox support they're the legitimate owner if the account gets reported or disputed.

Two listings, same pattern, same seller, both sitting in an active Discord server right now.

posts.title: Venice AI takes ordinary dollars for AI inference. Then it routes $5 of every $100 of credits sold into buying and burning its own token.
posts.author: Giants Tokenomics Labs
posts.snippet:
Venice AI takes ordinary dollars for AI inference. Then it routes $5 of every $100 of credits sold into buying and burning its own token.

Buyers who want nothing to do with crypto never touch it. Token holders get paid anyway.

That fiat bridge is the most copyable part of the VVV/DIEM design, and almost nobody copies it.

The rest: staking VVV buys a pro-rata share of Venice's API capacity. Locking that stake mints DIEM — an ERC-20 paying $1.00/day of inference credit, forever, whether you use it or sell it. A subscription turned into a bearer asset.

Issuance is governed by a curve, not a committee:

MintRate = 90 · e^(2·(S/38,000)³)

At the 38,000 target that's 665 sVVV per DIEM — ~$7,890 to mint $365/year of credit. Near the cap buying beats minting: the curve throttles supply until GPU capacity catches up.

The record isn't clean. ATH $22.58 on listing day, then −96% to $0.92 by December 2025. The recovery to $11.86 (~$563M) tracks the DIEM launch, three burn paths, and emissions cut 14M → 3M/yr — eighteen months of corrections, not a new narrative.

What transfers: denominate the instrument in units of service, cap issuance to real capacity, fund burns from fiat revenue, sequence demand before the token — Venice had 100k+ users, no presale, no VC.

What doesn't: it presumes a commodity. "1% of GPU capacity" is a coherent claim. 1% of a trading signal is not — exclusive information decays when distributed.

Full mechanics and the liability mismatch in the article.

- Sep 22, 2025 - “Jade from People Share” sends fake job text
- Sep 30, 2025 - Ghost text promoting investment via s.srax.com link
- Oct 15, 2025 - “Resource Logistic” sends fake job email
- Aug 1, 2026 - qp-mail delivers fake SSA email directly to inboxes

- Lack of proactive detection - most action still happens only after victims report the fraud (zero benefit to victims)
- No accountability measures in place for the loss of income experienced by job seekers
- Weak cross-border enforcement when the actual operators are overseas
- No requirement for registrars to flag or block domains used in SMS phishing or government impersonation campaigns

posts.title: Jonathan Goodman kept his keys on a device that lived in a safety deposit box and never touched the internet. On July 29, he watched 18.25 BTC leave every wallet he owned inside se
posts.author: Stefan Lauer
posts.snippet:
Jonathan Goodman kept his keys on a device that lived in a safety deposit box and never touched the internet. On July 29, he watched 18.25 BTC leave every wallet he owned inside seven minutes.

Nothing about his setup failed. The #Coldcard bug sat one layer earlier, in the second where a device asks a chip for random numbers and turns them into a recovery phrase. A build-flag check in the March 2021 firmware tested whether a setting existed rather than whether it was enabled, so seed generation quietly fell through to the software. That left roughly 40 bits of entropy on the Mk3 against the 128 a standard phrase should carry. At 128 bits, guessing is physically impossible; at 40, it is an afternoon with rented hardware.

Galaxy Research documented 1,367.05 BTC being swept from addresses that had been dormant for an average of 3.18 years. Coinkite shipped a fix within days and owned the failure publicly, but no patch reached the key material that was already predictable.

I count at least five versions of this same bug since the Android RNG flaw of 2013, and every one of them lived in open code that anybody could have read. Randomness is the least glamorous line in any crypto product, and it is the only one nobody can fix later.

I wrote up for Coinpedia.org what the incident actually broke and what it left standing: https://lnkd.in/dYPtD_hY
posts.reason: Detailed technical forensic analysis of Coldcard RNG failure with concrete loss figures (1,367 BTC) and root-cause explanation—exactly the kind of substantive incident discussion that interests law enforcement, exchanges, and insurers.

comments.text: The distinction worth stressing is that 'cold' only describes network exposure, not entropy quality - a device can never touch the internet and still produce a predictable key if the RNG path silently degrades.
Do we know yet whether Coinkite's fix included a way for users to verify retroactively whether their specific device batch fell into the affected entropy range, short of moving funds?

In tracing cases involving compromised seed generation, the giveaway is almost always the same as here - dormant wallets suddenly swept within minutes, which is a very different signature from a phishing-led theft.

posts.title: Holding seized crypto is a completely different problem than holding any other seized asset.
posts.author: Haven256
posts.snippet:
Holding seized crypto is a completely different problem than holding any other seized asset. 

Evidence rooms were built to secure physical items like firearms and cash. Unlike tangible goods, crypto can literally vanish if someone mishandles a seed phrase.

South Korea just learned that lesson the hard way… twice. In January, roughly 320 BTC (about $48 million) vanished from the Gwangju District Prosecutors' Office after a staff member entered wallet credentials into a phishing site during a routine verification. The loss had actually occurred months earlier, but went undetected due to inadequate management systems. Shortly after, a nationwide audit revealed that an additional 22 BTC had also gone missing from the Gangnam police. Both incidents involved USB-based cold wallet setups sitting in sealed vaults. Cold wallet storage is generally a good practice, but as it turns out, it protects the device, not the assets.

The custody of digital assets is a specialist function. It requires key management, continuous monitoring, incident response that runs around the clock, and a balance sheet capable of absorbing a loss when something goes wrong.

That’s why, at HAVEN256, we’re building the all-in-one custody oversight platform for managing seized digital assets.

To learn more, check out our website. Links are in the comments below.

posts.title: 🔒 📝 Coldcard victims pay to leave traces inside the hacker’s Bitcoin wallet.
posts.author: Crypto Economy
posts.snippet:
🔒 📝 Coldcard victims pay to leave traces inside the hacker’s Bitcoin wallet.

The address linked to the Coldcard exploit has turned into an unexpected public message board on the Bitcoin blockchain. Since the attack began, affected users have started sending small amounts of BTC alongside messages directed at the attacker, permanently recording their words on-chain.

The wallet identified by Galaxy Research as controlled by the attacker holds around $36 million in stolen bitcoin and has received multiple messages through OP_RETURN, a native Bitcoin feature that allows data to be embedded into transactions.

The messages reveal a mix of desperation, negotiation, and unrelated activity. Some victims plead for the return of their funds or include addresses where stolen BTC could potentially be sent back. Others demand specific portions of their lost holdings.

Not every message is connected to the exploit. Some users have used the public attention around the wallet to offer services to the attacker, including bitcoin laundering proposals, while others simply left messages unrelated to the theft.

The situation echoes the use of OP_RETURN during the LuBian mining pool hack in 2020, when users attempted to contact attackers after more than 127,000 BTC were stolen.

The Coldcard exploit has become one of the most significant self-custody security incidents in recent years, with confirmed losses exceeding $100 million.

Beyond the attack itself, the episode highlights one of Bitcoin’s defining characteristics: once information is recorded on the blockchain, it remains permanently visible on a network designed to resist censorship.
posts.reason: Discusses a major self-custody security incident with forensic evidence (wallet tracking, on-chain messages) that would interest compliance and law enforcement audiences we target.

We've traced funds through wallets carrying exactly this kind of noise - genuine victim pleas mixed with laundering solicitations - and the practical lesson is that none of it changes the tracing methodology, it just adds volume to sort through.

posts.title: Your hardware wallet can be perfectly offline and you could still lose everything. 🔐
posts.author: OAX Foundation
posts.snippet:
Your hardware wallet can be perfectly offline and you could still lose everything. 🔐

That is the uncomfortable lesson from the #Coldcard incident. Nobody picked up a device. Nobody broke in remotely. The flaw was in how the keys were made in the first place. 🚫

A firmware bug shipped in March 2021 caused seed phrases to be generated with far too little randomness. A properly generated seed is effectively a 39 digit number, roughly the number of atoms in the planet. On affected devices, it was 13 digits.

So the attacker did not guess anything. They simply generated every seed those devices could have produced, checked which ones held BTC, and helped themselves. 😅

📉 #Galaxy Research tracked around 1,367 $BTC, close to US$89 million, swept from about 4,585 addresses across three waves. The first wave alone drained 1,083 BTC in roughly 41 minutes.

The part worth sitting with: every wallet emptied in that first wave was single signature.

What this changes for anyone holding self custody:

✅ Use a strong BIP-39 passphrase. For many holders, that was the difference between exposure and safety.
✅ Do not concentrate everything with one vendor. A single bug should not be a single point of total failure.
✅ Consider multisig for meaningful balances.
✅ Where your device offers user supplied randomness (dice rolls, for example), use it.
✅ Actually subscribe to your vendor's security channels. The people who moved fastest here were the ones who saw the advisory early.

"Not your keys, not your #crypto" is still true. But it comes with a footnote most of us skip: your keys are only as good as the code that created them.

posts.title: I talk about this a lot, but it's true: Separate property claims are preserved by forensic tracing, not narrative.
posts.author: Peter Stambleck
posts.snippet:
I talk about this a lot, but it's true: Separate property claims are preserved by forensic tracing, not narrative.

In the Second Department decision Finley v. Turner, the appellate court reversed a ruling that attempted to absorb a $1.02 million account into the marital pool. The court restored $552,000 as separate property because an expert forensic audit established a paper trail.

New York law presumes ALL assets are marital. Overcoming that presumption requires an actual course of conduct backed by strict documentary evidence. If the tracing is fragmented, the asset integrity is compromised, and trouble starts. 

Judges rule on verifiable numbers. If the document trail fails, the marital presumption wins by default.
posts.reason: Family law attorney discussing forensic tracing methodology relevant to divorce litigation, one of our service areas, but narrow domestic audience with limited commercial reach.

comments.text: Finley v. Turner is a good reminder that the presumption isn't rebutted by testimony about intent — it's rebutted by an unbroken documentary chain, and a single unexplained gap can collapse the whole separate-property claim.

In cases where part of the original separate account was later commingled with crypto assets, does the same strict tracing standard apply, or do courts still treat on-chain records as inherently less reliable than bank statements?

We increasingly see this exact issue arise when one spouse's separate funds were converted into crypto at some point — without a forensic reconstruction of the wallet history, the presumption of marital property wins by default, just as you describe with bank accounts.

posts.author: Vladi Lepi

In 2018, a 260-year-old auction house did something unusual. It convened a conference and named one technology as the trend of the year, then let people argue about it in public, on its own stage, with a question in the title: Is the Art World Ready For Consensus?

The technology was blockchain. The following year the subject was artificial intelligence. In 2021 came the $69.3 million Beeple sale, and within eighteen months every other major house had followed Christie's into a category it had named first.

That is what a trend-setting institution does. It convenes a field, names its subject, and the field organizes around the naming. Which is why the 2026 edition is worth reading carefully. This year's subject was new wealth.

On 16 July, at Christie’s Art+Tech Summit in New York, the keynote discussion asked whether the fortunes now emerging from A.I. and space-industry IPOs will produce a new generation of art collectors. It is the right question. It is also only half of one - because a person with money is not yet a collector, and the more interesting question is not whether they will buy, but what they will buy.

Of a program running from 9:25 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., approximately thirty minutes went to technology as an artistic medium. Around six percent of the day. That is our own count, and two other publications counted the room the same way.

We are not arguing against Christie's position. We are restating the position Christie's took in 2018 — from its own stage, in its own words, by its own specialist — and asking why it is no longer the one being made.

The new collectors arriving now will be offered two things: physical art or digital art. There is a third, and it already has museum acquisitions, a section on the main floor of the world's largest art fair, and artists whose work does not exist without it. What it does not have is a line in the auction category system, which is exactly where a new buyer looks first.

Our full analysis is published today: what the summit could have done, what this house already built and largely forgotten, and why the category question is the one to watch before December.

An institution that convenes a field also sets its agenda. When the direction of that agenda reverses, saying so is not an attack. It is the only useful response available to the people working in the field it convened.

We would rather be argued with than simply agreed with. If you were in the room on 16 July - or if you build, collect, curate, or sell at the intersection of art, technology, and commerce - tell us where our reading is right or wrong. Ask questions and comment. Join the conversation.

posts.snippet: SKANFOREST Digital Forensic Evidence System and Humanitarian Aid Foundation Skanforest comprises two principal, interlinked Chilean initiatives: a technology company focused on digital forensic security and a humanitarian aid foundation for disaster response. Skanforest's Main Areas ● SKANFOREST SpA (Technology platform): Develops hardware, firmware and governance systems designed to generate digital evidence with cryptographic, verifiable sealing (such as the EvidencePack data packages). ● SKANFOREST.org (Foundation): A Chilean social organization focused on wildfire prevention and on the delivery of humanitarian aid during emergencies and post-disaster situations, using blockchain traceability for fund transparency. SKANFOREST SpA's digital evidence system produces mathematically verifiable, highly tamper-resistant computer evidence for judicial proceedings through advanced cryptography and sealing technologies. The following describes how its core technical unit operates and its legal grounding in Chile: The "EvidencePack v4.8" Package The company's core solution consists of packaging the collected evidence in a protected format called EvidencePack v4.8. It is characterized by: ● 7 Validation Layers: The system applies seven layers of international validation that operate in parallel. ● Resistance to Challenges: If a court-appointed expert or an opposing party disputes the validity of one layer, the remaining six continue to uphold the integrity of the package. ● Hardware and Firmware Infrastructure: It is not merely software; the company builds the physical components and the low-level code (firmware) required to shield the data from the moment of capture. Legal Basis in the Chilean Justice System The system's technical architecture is designed to align strictly with the legal framework governing Chilean courts. The canonical v4.8 schema is validated under the indivisible pair of procedural rules: ● Article 187 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CPP): Governs the lawfulness and proper safekeeping of the objects or documents collected during an investigation. ● Article 297 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CPP): Establishes the principles for weighing evidence in accordance with the rules of sound judicial reasoning (logic, scientific knowledge and the maxims of experience). A single intact validation layer is enough for the package to meet the standards of judicial admissibility required by the courts.

posts.title: I attended TDI Tech Summit expecting to take notes.
posts.author: Abasienyene Ekperikpe
posts.snippet:
I attended TDI Tech Summit expecting to take notes.

Instead, I ended up introducing Blockchain Forensics to a room of 1,000+ people. 

I had no prepared speech, no prior notice, and no expectation that I would be called to speak.

When the opportunity came, I shared my journey from Forensic Science into Blockchain Forensics & Web3 Security, and how investigative thinking can be applied to blockchain, digital investigations, and security awareness.

What happened next honestly surprised me.

Many people had never heard of Blockchain Forensics before. The moment I mentioned that I have a Forensic Science background and now focus on a field that combines forensics, blockchain investigations, and Web3 security, the curiosity in the room became impossible to ignore.

After the session, several attendees came up to me to ask:

• “Blockchain Forensics is actually a real niche?”
• “I have a Biochemistry degree. Do you think I can still transition into Blockchain Forensics and Web3 Security?”
• “How can I get started in this field?”

That second question stayed with me.

It reminded me that many people believe their degree determines the limits of their future, but technology is creating spaces where curiosity, consistency, and transferable skills matter just as much as your original field of study.

My phone has been filled with messages ever since, and I’m still trying to process how one unexpected moment created so many meaningful conversations. 

This experience taught me something important:

Your most unusual combination of skills may be the very thing that opens doors you never expected.

Thank you to TDI Tech Summit for creating a space where stories, curiosity, and technology could intersect in such a powerful way.

I left the event with more gratitude, more confidence, and an even stronger commitment to growing in Blockchain Forensics, Digital Investigations, and Web3 Security. 

#BlockchainForensics #Web3Security #DigitalForensics #techcommunity

Every organization faces risk, whether it's a startup, a multinational company, a financial institution, or even a small business. The difference between organizations that thrive and those that struggle often lies in how they identify, assess, and respond to those risks.

One common misconception is that risk management is about eliminating all risks. In reality, that's almost impossible. The goal is to anticipate potential threats, understand their impact, and put effective measures in place to minimize their likelihood and consequences.

In today's digital world, technology has transformed how businesses operate, but it has also introduced new risks that cannot be ignored. Some of the most common technology related risks include:

🔹Data Breaches: Unauthorized access to sensitive customer or business information.

🔹 Human Error: Simple mistakes, such as clicking phishing links, weak passwords, or accidental data deletion, can have serious consequences.

🔹Cyber Attacks:  Ransomware, malware, phishing, and other cyber threats continue to evolve, targeting organizations of all sizes.

🔹System Failures: Hardware failures, software bugs, or network downtime can disrupt operations and lead to financial losses.

🔹Poor Access Management: Granting excessive privileges or failing to revoke access for former employees can expose an organization to unnecessary risks.

Effective Risk Management is not just the responsibility of the IT or Compliance team, it's a shared responsibility across every department. Building a culture of security awareness, following established policies, and regularly reviewing potential risks are essential steps toward protecting an organization's people, data, reputation, and long-term success.

As someone who is passionate about Technology, Compliance, and Risk Management, I'm continually learning how proactive risk management strengthens business resilience and builds trust with customers and stakeholders.

One lesson I've learned is this:

You cannot always prevent every risk, but you can prepare for it. Preparation often makes the difference between a minor incident and a major crisis.

posts.title: A hacker steals $200M in stablecoins. Within hours, it's converted into a token that can never be frozen. That's the new speed you're up against.
posts.author: Ricardo Argudin
posts.snippet:
A hacker steals $200M in stablecoins. Within hours, it's converted into a token that can never be frozen. That's the new speed you're up against.

Every fraud department I talk to right now is having some version of the same conversation. "We finally got our transaction monitoring rules tuned. Then treasury started moving money in stablecoins."

I get it. For years, fraud programs were built around a predictable set of rails: card networks, ACH, wires, maybe real time payments if you were ahead of the curve. Stablecoins and tokenized assets don't play by those rules. They move 24/7, settle in seconds, cross borders without a correspondent bank in sight, and increasingly, they're the rail criminals prefer.

The numbers back this up. FATF's most recent reporting puts stablecoins at roughly 84% of illicit virtual asset transaction volume in 2025, with tens of billions tied to fraud and scams alone. And the typologies are evolving fast. When issuers freeze wallets, bad actors are now racing to convert into unfreezable tokens through decentralized exchanges within hours of a hack or exploit. Some criminal networks are even experimenting with their own proprietary stablecoins built specifically to resist seizure.

Here's what this means for fraud and compliance teams: rule based monitoring alone can't keep up. A static threshold that flags "large transfer to new wallet" doesn't tell you anything about intent. What matters now is behavior. How does this wallet's activity compare to its own history? Is this the kind of rapid, freezable to unfreezable conversion pattern we've seen after major exploits? Does the sequencing, timing, and counterparty pattern look like a human treasury operation or an automated laundering script?

This is exactly where behavioral analytics earns its keep. Instead of asking "did this transaction cross a threshold," the better question is "does this look like this entity, acting like itself." That shift, from static rules to adaptive behavioral baselines, is the difference between catching a laundering chain in hours versus reading about it in a regulator's report six months later.

The institutions that get ahead of this aren't the ones bolting crypto monitoring onto legacy systems as an afterthought. They're the ones rethinking detection as a behavioral problem first and a rails problem second.

Curious how other fraud and compliance leaders are adapting their programs as tokenized payments scale. What's changing first for you, the technology stack or the typologies you're watching for?

#FinancialCrime #FraudPrevention #Stablecoins #AML #BehavioralAnalytics #DigitalAssets
posts.reason: Deep technical analysis of stablecoin fraud typologies, monitoring challenges, and behavioral analytics directly addresses concerns of compliance officers and fraud teams we want to reach.

comments.text: The freeze-to-unfreezable conversion window you describe is exactly the choke point that matters in practice - once funds clear a DEX into a non-custodial or privacy-preserving asset, the realistic recovery path narrows fast, sometimes to nothing. Speed of detection, not sophistication of the eventual monitoring rule, is usually the deciding factor.

When you talk to fraud teams, are they tracking wallet-level behavioral baselines pre-incident, or only building them reactively after an exploit? That seems to be the real gap - baseline drift detection needs history you don't have if you start post-hack.

In tracing work across BTC, ETH and Tron we consistently see the same race: centralised exchange choke-points get flagged within hours, but stablecoin conversions through DEXs erase that leverage almost as fast as it appears. Static thresholds miss that because the anomaly isn't the amount, it's the timing relative to a known exploit.

One of the most significant responsibilities I have as a member of the House Education Committee is participating in Arkansas's biennial Educational Adequacy Study.

This work goes beyond reviewing a budget.

It is the Legislature's constitutional responsibility -- established following the Arkansas Supreme Court's Lake View decision -- to determine whether Arkansas is providing every student with an adequate and equitable public education.

The preliminary report released this week recognizes meaningful progress over the past two decades, including improvements in teacher compensation and student achievement.

At the same time, it identifies important challenges that remain, including:
• Student achievement that continues to lag national averages on NAEP. • No student subgroup meeting the state's long-term academic proficiency goals. • Significant unmet needs identified by school leaders in special education, student mental health, school safety, and dyslexia support. • Increasing reliance on local and other funding sources to provide educational resources.

Over the coming weeks, members of the House and Senate Education Committees will review the study, meet with stakeholders, and submit recommendations by August 24 to help guide education funding and policy for the next biennium.

I look forward to hearing from educators, parents, business leaders, and community members throughout this process.

Thoughtful public input strengthens good public policy.

Over the next several weeks, I'll also share information explaining how Arkansas funds public education, how the adequacy process works, and what these findings may mean for our state's future.

Recently, I spoke at an event attended by over 400 professionals, most of them public servants. During the Q&A, someone asked me a powerful question:

“Can someone working in the public sector also build an alternative source of income?”

The truth is, they must.

The rising cost of living is outpacing salary growth, and for many in the public sector, the gap is even wider.

It’s no surprise that some employees, when faced with financial pressure, may be tempted to mishandle public funds.

But I believe there’s a better path.

 There are legitimate ventures that do not conflict formal job, like starting a small farm to provide food for your family and generate some extra income from the surplus.

Someone can also sell a product or service, or turn a skill or hobby into a side hustle

We saw this clearly when USAID froze funding, and several Ministry of Health staff were asked to step aside or continue working voluntarily.

The big question is: How do you survive such storms if your only source of income disappears overnight?

It’s time we embraced a new mindset: grow your career, yes, but also create alternative sources of income.

 It’s not just about wealth creation; it’s about survival and creating your resilience in uncertain times.
